SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) and DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) are two types of volatile memory technologies used in computers to store data and program code.

SRAM uses a flip-flop circuit to store each memory cell, which requires four to six transistors. A flip-flop is a circuit that can store one bit of data and maintain it until a new bit of data is written. Each SRAM cell is made up of two cross-coupled inverters, which form a latch. The latch can hold a stable value of 1 or 0, depending on the input provided to it. The access time of SRAM is faster than DRAM because there is no need to refresh the data periodically.

A typical SRAM memory cell structure consists of two inverters with two access transistors as shown below:
```lua
                +--------+
                |        |
                |   Q    |
                |        |
                +---+----+
                |   |    |
                |   +----+------- Word line
                |        |
                |   Q    |
                |        |
                +--------+
```
The bit stored in the SRAM cell is determined by the state of the two inverters. The access transistors control the flow of data between the inverters and the bit line, which is connected to the input/output of the memory cell.

DRAM, on the other hand, uses a capacitor to store each memory cell. Each DRAM cell consists of a transistor and a capacitor. The transistor acts as a switch to control the flow of charge to and from the capacitor. When the transistor is turned on, the capacitor is charged or discharged, depending on the input provided to it. The data stored in the capacitor gradually fades away and needs to be refreshed periodically to maintain its state.

A typical DRAM memory cell structure consists of a transistor and a capacitor as shown below:
```lua
                +--------+
                |        |
        Word    |   T    |
        line    |        |
        +-------+    C   |
        |       |        |
        |       +--------+
        |
    Bit line
```
The bit stored in the DRAM cell is determined by the charge stored in the capacitor. The transistor controls the flow of charge to and from the capacitor, depending on the input provided to it. The access time of DRAM is slower than SRAM because it requires periodic refresh cycles to maintain the data in the capacitor.

In summary, SRAM and DRAM differ in the way they store data and the access time required to retrieve the data. SRAM uses flip-flop circuits to store data, while DRAM uses capacitors. SRAM has a faster access time than DRAM, but DRAM requires periodic refresh cycles to maintain the data.
explain transistor and capacitor in detail

Transistors and capacitors are two fundamental electronic components used in a wide variety of electronic devices.

A transistor is a semiconductor device that can amplify or switch electronic signals. It consists of three layers of doped semiconductor material - an emitter, a base, and a collector. The base region is typically very thin and lightly doped, while the emitter and collector regions are heavily doped. The transistor is designed such that a small current flowing into the base can control a much larger current flowing between the emitter and collector. This allows the transistor to act as an amplifier or switch.

In an NPN transistor, for example, when a positive voltage is applied to the base, it attracts free electrons from the emitter into the base region, forming a narrow region of negative charge. This decreases the width of the base region, increasing the electric field across it, which in turn causes more electrons to be injected from the emitter into the collector. As a result, a large current flows between the emitter and collector. When no voltage is applied to the base, the transistor is off and no current flows.

A capacitor is a passive two-terminal electronic component that stores electrical energy in an electric field. It consists of two conductive plates separated by a dielectric material, such as air or plastic. When a voltage is applied across the plates, an electric field is established between them. The capacitor stores energy in the electric field as a function of the applied voltage and the size of the plates. The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the distance between the plates, the area of the plates, and the dielectric constant of the material between the plates.

When a voltage is applied across the capacitor, the positive charge accumulates on one plate, and the negative charge accumulates on the other plate. The amount of charge that accumulates is proportional to the voltage applied and the capacitance of the capacitor. When the voltage is removed, the capacitor can discharge through a load, such as a resistor or an LED. The time it takes for a capacitor to discharge is determined by the resistance of the load and the capacitance of the capacitor.

In summary, transistors and capacitors are two important electronic components used in electronic devices. Transistors can amplify or switch electronic signals, while capacitors store electrical energy in an electric field. Both components have unique properties that make them essential for the design and operation of electronic circuits.

The JK flip-flop has two inputs (J and K), a clock input (CLK), and two outputs (Q and Q'). It can be used to implement more complex logic functions than the D flip-flop.

Instruction pipelining is a technique used in modern processors to improve performance by allowing multiple instructions to be processed concurrently. The technique involves dividing the execution of an instruction into several stages that can be executed in parallel. Each stage performs a specific operation on the instruction, and the pipeline moves the instructions from one stage to the next until the instruction has been fully executed. This approach allows for the overlapping of instructions, resulting in faster overall execution.

The stages involved in pipelining depend on the architecture of the processor. However, the stages in a typical RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor include:

1. Instruction Fetch (IF): The instruction is fetched from memory and loaded into the instruction register.
2. Instruction Decode (ID): The instruction is decoded to determine the operation to be performed and the operands involved.
3. Execution (EX): The instruction is executed using the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) and other functional units to perform the operation.
4. Memory Access (MEM): The instruction accesses memory to read or write data.
5. Write Back (WB): The result of the instruction is written back to the register file.

With pipelining, multiple instructions can be in different stages of execution simultaneously. For example, while the first instruction is being executed in the EX stage, the second instruction can be decoded in the ID stage, and the third instruction can be fetched in the IF stage. This overlap results in an increase in the overall throughput of the processor and improved performance.

However, pipelining can introduce some challenges as well. One common problem is the possibility of data hazards. Data hazards occur when an instruction depends on the results of a previous instruction that has not yet completed its execution. These dependencies can lead to pipeline stalls or bubbles, where the pipeline must wait for the previous instruction to complete before continuing, resulting in a reduction in performance.

To address these issues, processors use techniques such as forwarding or register renaming. Forwarding allows the result of an instruction to be passed directly to the next instruction, bypassing the need to wait for the result to be written back to the register file. Register renaming allows the processor to create additional registers, making it possible to assign new names to the registers that hold intermediate values, avoiding potential data hazards.

In summary, instruction pipelining enhances system performance by allowing multiple instructions to be processed concurrently, improving overall throughput. Although it can introduce challenges such as data hazards, these challenges can be addressed through techniques such as forwarding and register renaming.

AMP systems, on the other hand, have a master processor and several slave processors. Each computer in the system has its own memory and I/O system, and they can communicate with each other through a network interface. There are two types of multicomputers: cluster systems and grid systems.

Cluster systems are a group of computers that are connected by a high-speed network and are designed to work together as a single system. Each computer in the cluster has its own operating system, and the applications are divided among the computers in the cluster. The cluster system provides high availability, fault tolerance, and scalability.

Grid systems, on the other hand, are a collection of heterogeneous computers that are connected by a network and are geographically distributed. The resources in a grid system are shared among the computers, and the users can access the resources through a web interface. The primary difference between multiprocessors and multicomputers is the way they are organized. Multiprocessors are organized as a single system with shared resources, while multicomputers are organized as multiple independent systems connected by a network.

Multiprocessors can achieve high performance by using parallel processing, which divides a task into smaller sub-tasks and distributes them among the processors. On the other hand, multicomputers can achieve high performance by using distributed computing, which divides a task into smaller sub-tasks and distributes them among the computers in the network.

Another difference is the communication between the processors or computers. In multiprocessors, the processors communicate with each other through a shared memory or a common bus. In multicomputers, the computers communicate with each other through a network.

In terms of scalability, multiprocessors can be limited by the number of processors that can be connected to the shared memory or bus. Multicomputers can be scaled up by adding more computers to the network.

In conclusion, both multiprocessors and multicomputers are designed to increase computational power and provide high-performance computing. The choice between the two architectures depends on the specific requirements of the application and the available resources.

Interrupt Driven I/O (Input/Output) is a method of data transfer in which the CPU (Central Processing Unit) can perform other tasks while waiting for I/O operations to complete. In this approach, the I/O device sends an interrupt signal to the CPU when it is ready to transfer data, and the CPU responds to the interrupt by suspending the current task and servicing the I/O operation.

Interrupt Driven I/O vs. Programmed I/O:
In Programmed I/O, also known as Polling I/O, the CPU continuously checks the I/O device's status to see if it is ready for data transfer. This approach wastes CPU time, as the CPU is idle while it waits for the I/O operation to complete. In contrast, in Interrupt Driven I/O, the CPU can perform other tasks while waiting for the I/O operation to complete, thereby improving system performance.

Types of Interrupts:
There are several types of interrupts in a computer system, including:

1. Hardware Interrupts: Hardware interrupts are generated by external hardware devices, such as I/O devices or hardware timers. When a hardware interrupt occurs, the CPU suspends the current task and services the interrupt.
2. Software Interrupts: Software interrupts, also known as traps, are generated by software programs, such as system calls or exceptions. When a software interrupt occurs, the CPU suspends the current task and services the interrupt.
3. Internal Interrupts: Internal interrupts are generated by the CPU itself, such as a divide-by-zero error or a memory access violation. When an internal interrupt occurs, the CPU suspends the current task and services the interrupt.
4. External Interrupts: External interrupts are generated by external sources, such as network events or user input. When an external interrupt occurs, the CPU suspends the current task and services the interrupt.

Interrupt Driven I/O is particularly useful in systems where multiple I/O devices are used simultaneously, as it allows the CPU to perform other tasks while waiting for I/O operations to complete. However, care must be taken to avoid conflicts when multiple interrupts are generated simultaneously. Interrupt priority schemes are often used to ensure that high-priority interrupts are serviced first, to avoid system errors or crashes.

In summary, Interrupt Driven I/O is an efficient method of data transfer that allows the CPU to perform other tasks while waiting for I/O operations to complete. It is an improvement over Programmed I/O, which wastes CPU time while waiting for I/O operations to complete. There are several types of interrupts in a computer system, including hardware interrupts, software interrupts, internal interrupts, and external interrupts. Interrupt priority schemes are often used to manage multiple interrupts and ensure system stability.

Read-Only Memory (ROM) is a type of non-volatile memory that is used to store permanent data or programs that cannot be altered by the user. There are several types of ROM, including magnetic and optical ROM, each with its own characteristics and uses.

Magnetic ROM:
Magnetic ROM is a type of read-only memory that is based on magnetic material. It is a non-volatile memory that retains data even when the power is turned off. Magnetic ROM is typically used in embedded systems, where a fixed program needs to be stored permanently. There are two main types of magnetic ROM:

1. Mask ROM:
Mask ROM is the most basic type of ROM, and it is produced by the manufacturer with the data already stored in the memory. It is called "mask" ROM because a mask is used during the manufacturing process to protect the areas that do not need to be programmed. The data is programmed by changing the electrical properties of the silicon substrate, which cannot be altered once the ROM has been manufactured.
2. Programmable ROM (PROM):
PROM is a type of magnetic ROM that can be programmed by the user after the manufacturing process. The user can program the memory using a device called a programmer, which applies high voltage to certain areas of the memory to alter the electrical properties of the substrate. Once programmed, the memory retains the data permanently.
3. Erasable PROM (EPROM):
EPROM is a type of magnetic ROM that can be erased and reprogrammed multiple times. It is programmed using the same method as PROM but can be erased using ultraviolet light. The EPROM chip has a small window that allows ultraviolet light to penetrate and erase the memory.
4. Electrically Erasable PROM (EEPROM):
EEPROM is a type of magnetic ROM that can be erased and reprogrammed using electrical signals. Unlike EPROM, EEPROM does not require ultraviolet light to erase the memory, and it can be erased and reprogrammed while still in the system. EEPROM is commonly used in computer systems to store BIOS settings and other data that needs to be retained even when the power is turned off.

Optical ROM:
Optical ROM is a type of read-only memory that uses a laser to read the data stored on the disc. The data is stored on the disc as a series of pits and lands, which represent 1s and 0s, respectively. There are two main types of optical ROM:

1. Compact Disc-Read Only Memory (CD-ROM):
CD-ROM is a type of optical ROM that is commonly used for storing software and other large data files. It can hold up to 700 MB of data and can be read by any CD-ROM drive. CD-ROM discs are not rewritable, and the data is permanently stored on the disc.
2. Digital Versatile Disc-Read Only Memory (DVD-ROM):
DVD-ROM is a type of optical ROM that is similar to CD-ROM but has a higher capacity and can store up to 8.5 GB of data. DVD-ROM discs are also read-only and cannot be rewritten. DVD-ROM drives are backward-compatible with CD-ROMs and can read both types of discs.

In conclusion, ROM is a type of non-volatile memory that is used to store permanent data or programs that cannot be altered by the user. There are several types of ROM, including magnetic and optical ROM, each with its own characteristics and uses. Magnetic ROM is available in four types, namely mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, and EEPROM. On the other hand, optical ROM is available in two types, namely CD-ROM and DVD-ROM.

Microprogrammed control units (MCUs) are a type of control unit used in computer processors. They are designed to be flexible and easily programmable, allowing for easy modification and customization of the processor's control flow.

The design of a microprogrammed control unit typically involves several components, including a microinstruction ROM, a control memory, a control unit, and a sequencing unit.

The microinstruction ROM is the heart of the microprogrammed control unit. It stores the microinstructions that define the control flow of the processor. Each microinstruction corresponds to a specific operation or set of operations that the processor can perform.

The control memory is a set of registers that store the current state of the processor. This includes things like the current instruction being executed, the contents of the various registers, and any flags or status bits that the processor uses to track its state.

The control unit is responsible for decoding the microinstructions stored in the microinstruction ROM and controlling the various components of the processor. It translates each microinstruction into a set of control signals that are sent to the various components of the processor.

The sequencing unit is responsible for controlling the order in which the microinstructions are executed. It determines which microinstruction should be executed next based on the current state of the processor and the control signals generated by the control unit.

The overall design of a microprogrammed control unit allows for easy modification and customization of the processor's control flow. By simply modifying the microinstructions stored in the microinstruction ROM, it is possible to change the behavior of the processor without having to modify the hardware itself. This makes microprogrammed control units a popular choice for applications that require a high degree of flexibility and programmability.

in the context of indian toll highways, what does DBFOT mean?

DBFOT is an acronym used in the context of highway construction and maintenance in India, and it stands for Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer.

Under the DBFOT model, private companies are responsible for designing, building, financing, operating, and maintaining a toll road for a specified period, typically 15 to 30 years. In exchange, the company receives toll revenue from the road users and is responsible for maintaining the road's condition during the specified period.

At the end of the contract period, the ownership and operation of the toll road are transferred back to the government. The DBFOT model is used to promote private investment in infrastructure development and improve the quality of road infrastructure in India.
and what does TOT mean?

TOT stands for Toll-Operate-Transfer, which is a model for the monetization of public-funded highways in India. Under this model, the government hands over the rights to collect tolls on an operational highway to a private entity for a specified period, usually 15-30 years.

The private entity pays the government a lump sum upfront as consideration for the transfer of toll collection rights. The private entity operates and maintains the highway during the concession period, collects toll revenue from the road users, and is responsible for the upkeep and maintenance of the highway.

At the end of the concession period, the ownership and operation of the highway are transferred back to the government. The TOT model is used to unlock the value of the existing highways and generate revenue for the government to fund new infrastructure projects.

whats the role of the change management executive?

The role of a Change Management Executive is to facilitate and manage organizational change initiatives, ensuring that they are effectively planned, executed, and embedded within the organization. The primary goal of this role is to minimize any disruptions, maximize employee engagement, and ensure that the organization achieves its desired outcomes from the change.

Key responsibilities of a Change Management Executive typically include:

1. Assessing the need for change: Identifying areas where change is necessary, either in response to external factors (e.g., market conditions, customer demands) or internal factors (e.g., process improvements, organizational restructuring).
2. Developing a change strategy: Defining the approach and timeline for implementing the change, as well as the expected benefits and potential risks.
3. Stakeholder engagement: Identifying key stakeholders, ensuring their involvement and support, and addressing any concerns or resistance to the change.
4. Communication planning and execution: Developing and executing a communication plan to inform and engage employees and stakeholders about the change, its benefits, and the process.
5. Training and support: Ensuring that employees have the necessary skills and resources to adapt to the change, providing training and support as needed.
6. Change implementation: Overseeing the execution of the change initiative, working with project managers, team leads, and other stakeholders to ensure a smooth transition.
7. Monitoring and evaluation: Tracking the progress and impact of the change, identifying any issues or obstacles, and adjusting the strategy as needed.
8. Sustaining the change: Ensuring that the change becomes a permanent part of the organization's culture and operations, and that any lessons learned are incorporated into future change initiatives.

A Change Management Executive must possess strong leadership, communication, and interpersonal skills, as well as a deep understanding of organizational behavior, project management, and change management principles.

Part 2:

What is a Contract Variation?

A contract variation is a change or adjustment to what has already been agreed to in the construction contract.

These include a change in the amount or cost of works, an increase or decrease in the work needed to be done, and changes to the scope of works.

Contract variations may be either instructed by the client, or proposed by the builder; but they must always be agreed upon by both parties. They should also be put into writing, whether the proposed changes pertain to the way things are done, the quality of work, or the costs.

Causes of Variations

There are several reasons why variations happen.

Variations may be caused by a council requirement or by unforeseen circumstances. They may also be caused by the builder or tradesperson’s fault – in which case, you won’t need to pay to rectify the defects or fix the problem.

Variations may also be caused by the homeowner’s request – as when they think of adding something to the building works after they’d already signed the construction contract.

Here are some specific examples:

Situation #1

A homeowner requests the builder to do additional work after realizing that the house may need another window.

Situation #2
A head contractor sees that some of the contractors’ work overlap; so the former decides to change the scope of works to better suit the contractors’ designated tasks.

Situation #3
A builder decides to change the quality of paint to be used for a paint job, because of a change of preference.

Situation #4
Sudden temperature changes that cause changes to the project site, leading to cost adjustments.

Situation #5
Supply chain issues, shortage of materials, and ever changing costs of construction materials that affect the prices stated in the contract.

Nevertheless, regardless of the reason for the variations, they must be made in writing, and agreed to by both parties, before implementation.

x^3 + ax^2 - x - a = (x^3 - x) + (ax^2 - a).

Notice that x can be factored out of the first two terms and a can be factored out of the last two terms:

(x^3 - x) + (ax^2 - a) = x(x^2 - 1) + a(x^2 - 1).

Now, we can factor out the common factor (x^2 - 1):

x(x^2 - 1) + a(x^2 - 1) = (x + a)(x^2 - 1).

The factored equation is:

(x + a)(x^2 - 1) = (x + a)(x + 1)(x - 1) = 0.

So, the solutions are x = -a, x = -1, and x = 1. Factoring is typically the least computationally expensive method when it is possible, as it requires only basic arithmetic operations and rearrangement of terms.

In today's world, remote-first companies are becoming more common, with teams distributed across different time zones. One of the main challenges of such organizations is effective communication. In this article, we will discuss the importance of asynchronous communication and its best practices.

1. How timezone can be an issue for remote-first company

1. Reflect on your experiences: Think about the things that have been most meaningful or fulfilling to you in your life. What values were most important to you in those experiences?
2. Consider your relationships: Think about the relationships that are most important to you and what values you hold dear in those relationships.
3. Identify your core values: Make a list of the values that are most important to you. These might include things like honesty, compassion, independence, fairness, or respect.

5. Put your values into action: Once you have identified and prioritized your values, try to incorporate them into your daily life. This might involve setting goals that align with your values, making decisions that reflect your values, or taking actions that demonstrate your values.

One real-time application that can benefit from FLYNN's classification is Image Recognition. The best suitable model for implementing Image Recognition is the Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) model.

In the SIMD model, multiple processing elements (PEs) receive the same instruction and operate on different data elements in parallel. This parallel processing of data elements makes SIMD an efficient model for image recognition.

The image recognition algorithm involves convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which consist of multiple layers that process the image data. In each layer, multiple operations are performed on the data elements, such as convolution, activation, and pooling. These operations can be parallelized and executed in parallel by multiple PEs in a SIMD model.

In the SIMD model, each PE can perform the same operation on different image pixels in parallel, which results in faster processing of the image data. Additionally, SIMD architectures can also be designed to handle vector operations, which are commonly used in image recognition algorithms, efficiently.

On the other hand, the Single Instruction Single Data (SISD) model, where a single processing element receives and executes a single instruction, is not suitable for image recognition because it cannot efficiently parallelize the processing of data elements. Similarly, the Multiple Instruction Multiple Data (MIMD) model, where each processing element receives and executes different instructions, can also lead to inefficiencies in image recognition because of the additional overhead of coordinating the execution of multiple instructions.

In conclusion, the SIMD model is the best fit for image recognition because of its ability to efficiently parallelize the processing of image data and handle vector operations.

What are the top 25 common types of contracts or agreements that get executed between parties?

There are many types of contracts and agreements that get executed between parties, and the most common ones will vary depending on the context and jurisdiction. Here's a list of 25 common types of contracts and agreements:

1. Sales Agreement: A contract between a buyer and a seller for the purchase of goods or services.
2. Lease Agreement: A contract between a property owner (lessor) and a tenant (lessee) for the rental of real property.
3. Employment Contract: A contract between an employer and an employee outlining the terms and conditions of employment.
4. Independent Contractor Agreement: A contract between a company and an independent contractor for the provision of services.
5. Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA): A contract between two or more parties to protect confidential information shared between them.
6. Partnership Agreement: A contract between two or more individuals or entities agreeing to conduct business together.
7. Shareholders Agreement: A contract between shareholders of a corporation outlining their rights, obligations, and the management of the company.
8. Franchise Agreement: A contract between a franchisor and a franchisee granting rights to operate a franchise business.
9. Licensing Agreement: A contract that allows one party to use the intellectual property of another party under specific terms and conditions.
10. Service Agreement: A contract between a service provider and a client detailing the services to be provided and the associated fees.
11. Loan Agreement: A contract between a lender and a borrower outlining the terms and conditions of a loan.
12. Promissory Note: A written promise by one party to pay a specified sum to another party under agreed-upon terms.
13. Purchase Order: A document issued by a buyer to a seller indicating the details of the goods or services to be provided.
14. Consulting Agreement: A contract between a consultant and a client outlining the scope of work, compensation, and other terms.
15. Joint Venture Agreement: A contract between two or more parties to collaborate on a specific project or business opportunity.
16. Non-Compete Agreement: A contract that restricts one party from engaging in certain competitive activities.
17. Release of Liability/Waiver: A contract in which one party agrees to relinquish their right to sue another party for potential claims.
18. Memorandum of Understanding (MOU): A non-binding agreement between two or more parties outlining their intentions and commitments in a collaborative effort.
19. Power of Attorney: A document that authorizes one person to act on behalf of another in legal or financial matters.
20. Commercial Lease Agreement: A contract between a landlord and a business tenant for the rental of commercial property.
21. Property Management Agreement: A contract between a property owner and a property manager for the management and maintenance of a property.
22. Distribution Agreement: A contract between a manufacturer or supplier and a distributor to sell or distribute products.
23. Construction Contract: A contract between a contractor and a property owner for construction, renovation, or repair work on a property.
24. Merger and Acquisition Agreement: A contract outlining the terms and conditions of a merger or acquisition between two or more companies.
25. Settlement Agreement: A contract in which parties agree to resolve disputes or claims outside of litigation.

Please note that this list is not exhaustive and is meant to provide a general overview of common contracts and agreements. Always consult with a legal professional to ensure the proper execution of contracts and agreements specific to your situation.

Android service vs foreground service for files upload, what is more reliable?

Both Android services and foreground services can be reliable for file uploads, but the choice between the two depends on the specific requirements of your application.

A regular Android service runs in the background and is generally used for performing long-running tasks that do not require user interaction. However, if the system is low on resources, the Android operating system may kill the service to free up resources.

On the other hand, a foreground service is a type of service that provides a persistent notification to the user and runs with a higher priority than regular services. It is often used for tasks that are critical to the user experience, such as playing music or recording audio. Foreground services are less likely to be killed by the operating system, but they may consume more battery life and CPU resources.

For file uploads, a foreground service might be more reliable because it runs with a higher priority and is less likely to be killed by the operating system. Additionally, it provides a persistent notification to the user, which can improve the user experience by keeping them informed of the upload progress.

However, if your application does not require a persistent notification or does not have critical requirements for file uploads, a regular service may be sufficient and may consume fewer resources.

Ultimately, the choice between an Android service and a foreground service depends on the specific requirements of your application and the trade-offs you are willing to make between reliability and resource consumption.

3. Click on the "Create alarm" button.
4. In the "Name" field, enter a descriptive name for your alarm, such as "Node Level Anomaly Rate Alert."

```bash
sum(rate(netdata.error_requests{type="anomaly"}[1m])) / sum(rate(netdata.requests[1m])) > 0.05
```

Kind (Kubernetes IN Docker) is another tool that allows you to create local Kubernetes clusters using Docker containers. It enables you to create a cluster with one or more worker nodes running inside Docker containers on your local machine.

2. Include the variable font file(s) in your app's assets folder.
3. Use the Typeface class to create a Typeface object from the variable font file, and set it as the typeface for the text view(s) or other UI elements that you want to use the variable font on.
4. To use the variable font's variations, you can use the setTypeface() method with a Typeface object that contains the variation you want to use.
5. To further customize the text appearance, you can use the setTextSize() method to set the text size, and the setLetterSpacing() method to set the letter spacing.

You need to cast the value returned by `$prod->get_price()` to float before calling the `number_format` function to ensure that the argument passed to `number_format` is a float.


`functions.php` is a WordPress theme file that contains PHP code and functions. To add code to a plugin, follow these steps:

1. Go to the WordPress dashboard and click on "Plugins" in the left sidebar.
2. Click on "Add New" and then "Upload Plugin".
3. Select the plugin file you want to upload and then click on "Install Now".
4. After the plugin is installed, activate it by clicking on the "Activate" link.
5. Now you can edit the plugin by going to "Plugins" in the left sidebar, then clicking on "Editor".
6. In the plugin editor, select the plugin you want to edit from the dropdown list.
7. Add the code you want to add to the plugin file and save the changes.

It's important to note that directly editing a plugin can affect the functionality of the site, so it's recommended to make a backup of the site before making changes. If you're not comfortable with editing code, it may be best to seek help from a developer or consult the plugin documentation.

1. Create a new folder in your plugin directory, for example `my-plugin`.

```php
function my_custom_api_filter( $args ) {
    $args['meta_query'][] = array(
        'key' => '_stock_status',
        'value' => 'instock',
        'compare' => '=',
    );
    return $args;
}
```
1. Save the `functions.php` file.
2. In your plugin's main file, add the following line of code to include the `functions.php` file:
```php
require_once( plugin_dir_path( __FILE__ ) . 'my-plugin/functions.php' );
```

List all of the technical product managers' everyday tasks. You should explain each task in detail and give specific examples to demonstrate what technical product managers need to do in each task.

As a technical product manager, there are several tasks you'll perform every day to ensure that your team is delivering a successful product that meets customer needs. Here are some examples:

1. Developing product requirements: A technical product manager's primary responsibility is to define the product requirements that will guide the development team. This means gathering customer feedback, market research, and other relevant data to create a clear product roadmap. The technical product manager will then prioritize features and requirements, and communicate them to the development team.

For example, a technical product manager working on a software product might create a user story that reads "As a user, I want to be able to export data to Excel so I can perform further analysis on my data." They'll then work with the development team to define the technical requirements needed to fulfill that user story, such as data formats and export options.

2. Collaborating with the development team: Technical product managers work closely with the development team to ensure that the product is developed in line with the product requirements. This means communicating progress updates, answering technical questions, and facilitating collaboration between different teams.

For example, a technical product manager might have daily stand-up meetings with the development team to review progress, discuss roadblocks, and set priorities for the day. They might also work with the UX/UI design team to ensure that the product meets customer needs and looks visually appealing.

3. Managing the product backlog: Technical product managers are responsible for managing the product backlog, which is a prioritized list of features and requirements that the development team will work on. This means continually reviewing and updating the backlog based on customer feedback, market trends, and other factors.

For example, a technical product manager might use tools like Jira or Trello to manage the product backlog. They might prioritize features based on customer feedback and market research, and then work with the development team to break down those features into smaller, more manageable user stories.

4. Conducting user research: Technical product managers work with customers to understand their needs and pain points. This means conducting user interviews, surveys, and other forms of research to gather insights that can inform product decisions.

For example, a technical product manager might conduct a user interview with a customer to understand how they use the product and identify areas for improvement. They might then share those insights with the development team to guide product development.

5. Analyzing product data: Technical product managers use data to understand how customers are using the product and identify areas for improvement. This means analyzing metrics such as user engagement, conversion rates, and customer feedback to identify trends and patterns.

For example, a technical product manager might use tools like Google Analytics or Mixpanel to track user behavior and identify patterns. They might use that data to identify areas for improvement, such as improving the onboarding process or simplifying the user interface.

6. Communicating with stakeholders: Technical product managers are responsible for communicating product updates and progress to stakeholders, such as executives, investors, and other team members. This means creating presentations, reports, and other materials that summarize product performance and progress.

For example, a technical product manager might create a quarterly report that summarizes product performance, customer feedback, and development progress. They might then present that report to the executive team to keep them informed and get their feedback.

In Scrum, the team typically uses relative estimation techniques to size their work items, such as user stories, tasks, or features. The most commonly used technique for this is Planning Poker, which involves the team members estimating the size of a work item by assigning a story point value to it. Story points are a relative measure of effort, complexity, and risk, rather than an absolute unit of time or effort.

The team estimates the work items during the Sprint Planning meeting, which is a time-boxed event that happens at the beginning of each Sprint. The team members collaborate to identify the work items they will commit to delivering during the upcoming Sprint, and they estimate their size using Planning Poker or other similar techniques. The team may also revisit their estimates during the Sprint if new information or changes arise.

In terms of who participates in estimation, the whole Scrum team is typically involved, including the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Development Team. The Product Owner provides context and clarifies the requirements, while the Development Team provides technical insights and estimates the work items. The Scrum Master facilitates the process and ensures that the team adheres to the Scrum framework.

Some Scrum teams may also use tools to support their estimation process, such as digital Planning Poker tools or collaborative whiteboard software. However, the use of such tools is not required, and the team can use simple physical cards or other means to facilitate the estimation process.

Overall, the Scrum team estimates the size of their work items using relative estimation techniques, such as Planning Poker, during the Sprint Planning meeting. The whole Scrum team participates in this process, and they may use tools to support their estimation process.

Purple Tansy

Free Gift Option One: Purple Tansy Seeds

Purple Tansy (Phacelia tanacetifolia), is also known as ‘Bee’s Friend’ and that is for good reason, it is considered a top honey plant, and bee hives placed in acres planted with Purple Tansy can produce 180-1500 lbs of honey per acre and 300-1000 lbs of light-blue pollen per acre. Because of the abundance of nectar and pollen that Purple Tansy produces, it has a special value to native bees who rely on these resources.

Purple Tansy attracts common species, mostly bumble bees, honey bees, mason bees, and syrphid flies. In my gardens, though I have also seen leafcutter bees, moths, and butterflies visit my Purple Tansy blooms.

Borage is a pretty important plant to both honey bees and bumblebees alike. Who will you be helping?
Local Honey Bees: to attract and help local honey bees, make sure you plant the seeds (these seeds or any nectar and pollen-producing seeds) in groupings of 6-8 plants. The reason for this is, like the rest of the designated jobs throughout their hives, honey bee foragers have designated pollen and nectar sources and will only collect resources from one type of source per forage trip. A single plant or plants in groups less than 6, in close proximity will be passed over by the honey bees who are looking for the most efficient areas to collect resources.

Bumblebee on Purple Tansy Bloom
Bumblebee on Purple Tansy Bloom
Native Bees: Unlike honey bees, native bee species will visit multiple pollen and nectar sources per trip and will happily visit individual or small groupings of plants. Some solitary native bee species will also use the plants as a home or place to rest and as shelter from rainy or cold weather, like the long-horn bee in the photo to the right who took up residence in my sunflower patch last summer. This little one would tuck itself in between the petals at sunset and begin its day with a grooming session as the sun rose and the temperatures warmed up. It would move from bloom to bloom as the sunflowers faded and lost their petals – make sure you seed in succession for continued blooms from August through to late September.

Hummingbirds: It’s not just honey bees and natives that will visit your garden, you’ll see hummingbirds as well! Most people associate hummingbirds with bright red liquid feeders but hummingbirds are pollinators too, and they love to visit flower and vegetable gardens sampling the different natural nectar sources. Hummingbirds are highly territorial and feeders can be a competitive place, by growing nectar-producing plants throughout your yard, you will be increasing the food resources over a larger and more spread-out area. Want to feed hummingbirds but not sure if they will visit sunflowers? The ones by my house sure do! I have three feeders up but the most hummingbird squabbles happen over my patch of sunflowers. Did you know that they will puff themselves up to the size and look of a golf ball, make a high-pitched war cry and charge their competitors? Neither did I until I saw it with my own eyes and then spent a few hours Googling it.

Painted Lady Butterfly
Painted Lady Butterfly
Butterflies & Moths: Butterflies and moths are pollinators as well and they eat nectar and pollen just like bees do, they also transfer the pollen from bloom to bloom the same way as bees, and some species even have pollen patches on their legs. Personally, I have always been fascinated by butterflies, I relate more to honey bees in their task orientation and butterflies always seem to be flitting about on a whim, wandering to and fro, but they make migration journeys that far outreaches any bee, and must require drive and direction.

Moths as well, seem to be overlooked and underrated, just take the hummingbird, bumblebee, and luna moths for example. The first two resemble hummingbirds and mimic hummingbird movements, they even feed during the day, collecting nectar from the same plants as hummingbirds. The luna moth is a brilliant bright green with creamy white markings that look like that of a butterfly, the wing shape even resembles a butterfly’s wings. They come out at night but can also be seen resting during the day.

Go The Extra Mile: Add a Watering Station
Pollinator Water Station
Pollinator Water Station
Although nectar is a fluid, pollinators still need a reliable source of clean, fresh, accessible water. Creating and maintaining one or several watering stations is quick and easy and will not only add interesting features but will bring life into your garden. You’ll love watching all of the different insect species collect water but also how they interact with each other and the effects of their presence on your nearby plants.

A watering station can be as simple as filling a birdbath with river pebbles or clean gravel. You can also use water trays meant to fit under flowerpots, doing the same, filling them with pebbles or gravel. You can use natural mosses along the edges or use pebbles to make a gradual slope, with a rise in the center. The important thing to keep in mind is that the water levels need to be kept shallow – the gravel or pebbles should break above the surface, this provides pollinators somewhere to land and if they fall in, they can get themselves out without drowning.
To avoid mosquito larvae, freshen the water every other day or so, also you will find that it will need to be refilled just as often since the water level is being kept low.

By adding some food sources, shelter, and water, you will be helping native pollinators and honey bees alike, and by doing so will make your garden a fascinating and magical place to spend time.

If you're one of those who appreciate the rich flavors and unique nuances of artisan honey, join us as we unveil the enchanting process behind harvesting this liquid gold.

The Art of Harvesting Honey
Harvesting honey requires patience, care, and a deep understanding of the bees and their hives. Beekeepers usually wait until the late summer or early fall, when the honey flow is at its peak, to begin the harvest. At this time, the bees have gathered an abundance of nectar from various blooms, creating honey with diverse flavors and hues.

Suit Up and Smoke Out
Beekeepers suit up in protective gear, including gloves and a veil, to ensure a safe honey harvest. A smoker is used to gently introduce smoke into the hive, which helps calm the bees and makes the process less disruptive for them. The smoke encourages the bees to gorge on honey, keeping them preoccupied and less likely to sting.

Uncapping the Frames
Once the frames are removed from the hive, the beekeeper carefully uncaps the honeycomb cells using a heated knife or uncapping tool. The uncapping process exposes the golden treasure within the wax cells, allowing it to be extracted.

Spinning the Sweetness
The frames are then placed in an extractor, which uses centrifugal force to spin the honey out of the comb. The honey drains to the bottom of the extractor, where it's collected and filtered to remove any beeswax, pollen, or other debris.

Savoring the Liquid Gold
The final step in the journey is bottling the honey, preserving its unique characteristics and flavors. Each jar of artisan honey represents the hard work of both the bees and the beekeeper, resulting in a delicious and natural sweetener that brings joy to those who savor it.

Honey Tasting 101: Savor the Nuances of Artisan Honey Like a True Connoisseur

There is an enchanting world hidden within each droplet of artisan honey, a realm of bewitching flavors and mesmerizing floral notes that sings of the passion of beekeepers and the tireless labor of buzzing bees. As a connoisseur of these delectable delights, one must learn to savor the nuances of artisan honey, appreciating the unique characteristics that make each batch an exquisite experience. So, gather your friends and embark on a journey through the captivating world of honey tasting.

Setting the Stage for a Honey Tasting Event
To create a magical honey tasting experience at home, begin by assembling a selection of artisan honeys. Aim for a variety of flavors and colors, from light and delicate acacia to bold and robust buckwheat honey. Arrange them on a beautiful platter or tray, accompanied by spoons or honey dippers for sampling.

Next, prepare an array of accompaniments that will enhance the honey's unique characteristics. A well-curated cheese board, featuring a mix of soft and hard cheeses, will complement the honey's sweetness. Fresh fruits, such as sliced apples, pears, and berries, provide a refreshing contrast to the honey's rich flavors. Don't forget to include crusty bread and assorted crackers for a delightful crunch.

Finally, set the scene with charming decor that reflects the enchanting essence of honey. Consider adorning your table with fresh flowers, beeswax candles, and bee-themed linens for a truly immersive experience.

The Art of Tasting Honey
With your honey tasting event set, it's time to dive into the magical world of artisan honey. To truly appreciate the subtle differences in flavor and texture, follow these steps:

Observe: Take note of the honey's color and consistency. A honey's hue can range from pale gold to deep amber, with the intensity of its flavor often increasing with the richness of its color.

Aroma: Breathe in the sweet fragrance of each honey, allowing its floral notes to dance upon your senses. Close your eyes and envision the blossoms visited by the bees, as the aroma paints a vivid olfactory landscape.

Taste: Using a clean spoon or honey dipper, place a small dollop of honey on your tongue. Let it linger, allowing the honey to work its magic across your taste buds. Savor the initial burst of sweetness, followed by the complex symphony of floral notes and the lingering aftertaste.

Pair: Experiment with different combinations of honey, cheese, fruits, and crackers. Discover the harmonious interplay between the various flavors and textures, as you create your own symphony of taste sensations.

Share: Encourage your friends to share their impressions and favorite pairings. Discuss the unique qualities of each honey, as you deepen your appreciation for the art of honey tasting.

As you explore the world of artisan

honey tasting, allow your senses to guide you on this enchanting journey. Delight in the myriad flavors and fragrances, and revel in the knowledge that you are not only savoring the fruits of nature's labor but also supporting the passionate artisans who dedicate their lives to this magical craft.

Tips for a Successful Honey Tasting Event
To ensure a truly memorable honey tasting experience, keep these tips in mind:

1. Serve honeys at room temperature, as chilling them may mute their flavors and make them more difficult to appreciate.
2. Begin your tasting with the lightest honey and progress to the darker, more robust varieties. This will allow your palate to adjust and fully appreciate the nuances of each type.
3. Provide palate cleansers, such as sparkling water or plain crackers, to help refresh your taste buds between tastings.
4. Encourage guests to cleanse their spoons or honey dippers between samples to avoid cross-contamination of flavors.
5. Consider providing a tasting sheet or journal for guests to record their impressions and favorite pairings, creating a keepsake of your enchanting honey tasting event.

By following these steps and embracing the art of honey tasting, you and your friends will forge a deeper connection with nature and its sweet bounty. As you savor the nuances of artisan honey, remember that each drop is a testament to the dedication of skilled beekeepers and the hard work of our beloved pollinators. So, raise your spoon in appreciation and toast to the magical world of artisan honey.
